text:
Simply : a vol $VIX spike = spring compresses. FAST vol collapse = spring snaps. Only a FAST snap is a good buy signal. The speed of the vol collapse back from high vol matters, not just that it falls. A spike by itself just tells you fear is rising. It tells you nothing about whether the fuel will be released fast enough to matter. You're waiting for the release, not the compression.
 
Here's why:
 
Fast vol collapse = forced buying in a burst
• When volatility spikes, traders get caught short "Delta" (they're short stock as a hedge).
• If vol then collapses quickly, all those traders are forced to buy back stock at roughly the same time — a big, concentrated burst of buying.
• That burst is what creates the sharp, meaningful bottom and the strong rebound. 
Slow vol decline = buying gets spread out and wasted
• If vol just grinds lower slowly, the forced Delta buying happens in small trickles over weeks or months.
• Each little bit of buying gets absorbed by sellers. There's no concentrated "wall" of demand.
• The "potential energy" never gets released all at once — it leaks out harmlessly. 
The analogy: Think of it like a compressed spring. A vol spike compresses the spring (builds potential energy). A fast release snaps the market upward. A slow release just lets the spring uncoil gently with no pop.
 
So the sequence that actually matters for a real bottom is:
1. Vol spikes hard (panic, fear, implied vol expands)
2. Vol collapses fast (fear drains quickly)
3. Forced Delta

text:
I covered this earlier in Jan regarding PCB bottlenecks with photonics + $AMZN Kuiper / $SPCX starlink supply chains.

But as an update, it like other industries outside of AI are really starting to feel the pain now too.  

Global Electronics Association: "Is issuing this Industry Alert on escalating shortages across the printed circuit board (PCB) supply chain. 

Companies in automotive, industrial, medical, defense, and telecommunications report longer lead times and difficulty securing supply as AI absorbs scarce capacity, effectively putting production at risk"

The association meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. The association urged buyers to plan ahead for supply constraints and manufacturers.

Hyperscalers like $AMZN already planned ahead of time taking stakes in Gold Circuit Electronics (2368) for supply procurement... 

But can't say the same about other industries procurement (medical industry is probably not used to competing with hyperscalers over the same supply lol). 

The resulting shortages of critical materials, including CCLs and fibreglass cloth, are squeezing supplies for consumer electronics.

TLDR: same bottleneck, same timeline for 2028. It's just interesting to see association warnings about it impacting medical to defense industries. 

So there's incremental information that it's become an industry wide allocation issue. 

I also think it's helpful to see escalating shortages + broadening... so it might show the selloff is starting to look v

text:
Anthropic’s IPO ($ANT) and private placement are expected to bring in about $105B after fees.

Its spending commitments run down the data center stack.

➡️ Firepower: The final prospectus puts pro forma cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments at $232.4B… 3.3x the $70.7B due in the 12 months following Sep 30, 2026.

➡️ The order book: About $901B in committed spending, nearly all compute and infrastructure. That includes $451B in signed leases that had not begun as of Sep 30… nine times the level at year-end 2025.

➡️ Who gets paid:

▪️ Custom silicon: about $161B in TPU equipment lease payments, excluding interest, through Broadcom and financing partners.

▪️ Clouds: at least $278.5B across Google, Amazon and Microsoft.

▪️ Other compute providers: up to $120.5B with SpaceX’s AI unit and up to approximately $86B across Nscale and Lambda.

The hardware spans TPUs, Trainium and NVIDIA GPUs, with AMD Helios capacity planned for 2027.

More on Anthropic’s IPO in today’s Tech Edge. Sign up via the link in the comments.

text:
Nvidia dispelled fears of the AI trade slowing with one simple number: FY28 revenue growth is guided to be 75%, up from 70%, despite a higher FY27 base. Rubin’s first quarter is nearly double Blackwell’s at $20B vs $11B.

But let’s talk about what’s on everyone’s minds – is the AI trade over? Or perhaps equally concerning, is AI slowing to the point the glory years are behind us?

Psychology is a major component of successful investing, and there is not a more important time to protect your mindset than when valuations are at a multi-year low. 

Case in point, you’d have to go back nearly a decade to find $NVDA trading at these multiples; therefore, it’s reasonable to assume that many years could go by before investors see some of these valuations again. 

With that in mind, below are five reasons we believe the current panic may be presenting investors with a rare buying opportunity, rather than signaling the end of the AI trade.
